title: Waking
hookLine: Modeh Ani before your feet touch the floor, every day this week
tomorrow: a fight last night. how do you start the day clean?

lines: BEFORE YOUR FEET TOUCH THE FLOOR.
cards: The alarm goes off, and a hand finds the phone before the eyes are fully open. Headlines, messages, someone else's vacation. The day has started, and it started with everybody else's voice.
Jewish tradition puts something in that gap, before your feet even touch the floor. One short Hebrew sentence, said lying down or sitting on the edge of the bed, eyes still heavy.
They're called Modeh Ani, and they are the first words of the day.

teach.h: I GIVE THANKS: MY SOUL RETURNED.
teach.b: Here's what Modeh Ani says, in plain English. I give thanks before You, living and lasting King, for You have returned my soul to me, with compassion. Great is Your faithfulness.
A woman says modah ani; a man, modeh ani. Same thanks. Notice what it's built around.
Not a request, not a plan for the day. Thanks, for something that happened while you weren't paying attention: you woke up.

teach.h: SLEEP LETS GO; WAKING HANDS IT BACK.
teach.b: Tradition reads sleep as a small letting go, and waking as the soul handed back. You didn't earn it overnight. It was returned.

And the last words, great is Your faithfulness, come straight from the book of Lamentations, a book of grief, where the writer says of God's mercies: "They are new every morning; great is Thy faithfulness."
One to tell a friend tonight: the morning thank-you borrows its ending from a book of grief. It means the thanks isn't only for good mornings.

teach.h: NO NAME OF GOD, SO SAY IT IN BED.
teach.b: Here's a small detail people notice: Modeh Ani has no name of God in it, only You. That's why, by custom, it can be said right away, before washing, still in bed. It's made to be the very first thing.
Some families teach it to toddlers, sung, before they can read. So this week, the line is easy to carry.
Before the phone, before the floor: first words, thanks.

how: On waking, Jews traditionally say Modeh Ani before getting out of bed (modah ani for women); children often learn it as a short song, and it is said before washing because it contains no name of God.

o: the night watch kept in the Temple until dawn
the alarm-clock ritual of checking your phone
the first moments of the day, met with thanks

p: so it can be said in bed

s: Modeh Ani is a request for a good day
it's thanks, not a request: for the soul handed back when you woke.
its last words echo the book of Lamentations
they are new every morning; great is Thy faithfulness. a thank-you borrowed from a book of grief.

games.q: a terrible night: you barely slept, and the day ahead is hard. does Modeh Ani still fit this morning?
o: yes; its ending comes from a book of grief, so it was never only for good mornings.
no; thanks is for mornings when you actually feel rested and happy.
only if you swap the thanks for a request to get through the day.
games.why: great is Your faithfulness comes from Lamentations, where the mercies are new every morning even in grief. the thanks is for waking at all.

practice: Sit on the edge of your chair the way you'd sit on the edge of a bed, feet just lifted off the floor, hands resting on your knees.
If you say it, say modeh ani or modah ani, softly, or the English; if not, say thank you for waking up, out loud. Then set both feet down slowly and feel the floor meet you.

wordCard.voice: Waking: Modeh Ani, the first words of a Jewish morning. Thanks for a soul handed back, before your feet touch the floor.

orig.note: Hebrew: I give thanks. A woman says modah ani (moh-DAH ah-NEE).
